narrative.text: States the learning objectives of the module: using immunization data to support operational, managerial, and strategic decisions at all levels, as well as programme monitoring and accountability.

Defines the scope and target audience for the routine immunization data analysis guidance, noting that separate guidance covers periodic multi-source reviews using surveys and focused investigations. The module targets Ministry of Health decision-makers (immunization programme staff, data managers, and HIS managers), immunization partner staff, and research institute consultants and staff.

Lists two suggested WHO reference documents: the February 2016 working draft 'Collecting, Assessing, and Using Immunization Data: Reference guide' and the 2015 'Data Quality Review: A toolkit for facility data quality assessment'.
Credits the key authors of Module 6—Jan Grevendonk, Robert Pond, and Alain Poy—along with the February 2018 working document running footer.

Presents the table of contents covering data scope, data quality, core facility indicators, and core analyses (coverage, dropouts, stock management, AEFIs, sessions, and reporting completeness), followed by acknowledgements of financial support from the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative, Gavi, the Global Fund, and Norad.

Describes the scope of routine facility immunization data covered by the guide—tracking child and maternal vaccinations, AEFIs, vaccine supplies, and cold chain status—while excluding campaign data, disease surveillance, case-based severe AEFI investigations, and HR/financial tracking. It explains how monthly aggregate reporting and Electronic Immunization Registries (EIRs) operate alongside integrated HMIS platforms such as DHIS2 and Excel-based tools like the District Vaccine Data Management Tool (DVDMT).

Outlines essential data quality assessment steps prior to analysing routine immunization data, combining desk reviews (using WHO's Excel DQR tool or DHIS2 Data Quality Tool) with field data verification surveys against facility registers and tally sheets. It details three core checks: assessing reporting completeness and timeliness, checking internal consistency (detecting outliers beyond 3 standard deviations, suspicious uniformity or multiples of 5/10, negative dropouts or wastage rates, and register discrepancies), and evaluating external consistency against population-based surveys such as DHS and MICS.
Contains the page header and running footer ('WORKING DOCUMENT, FEBRUARY 2018 – 10 –') marking the transition to Section 3 on core facility indicators.

Tabulates the core health facility immunization indicators, their calculation formulas, and required disaggregations across seven areas: immunization coverage rate by vaccine, dropout rates (DPT1–DPT3, BCG–MCV1, and MCV1–MCV2), closed and open vial wastage rates, full availability of vaccines and supplies, functional status of cold chain equipment, temperature alarms, serious and non-serious AEFIs, and immunization session completion rate.
Displays the section heading continuation fragment ('SCHEDULE') for the core analysis subsection on immunization coverage for each vaccine in the national schedule.

Defines immunization coverage as the percentage of a target population vaccinated with a defined number of antigen doses and explains its use across facility, sub-national, and national levels. It catalogues nine standard coverage and dose-monitoring visualizations (Charts/Maps 1–9), including cumulative facility coverage charts, district coverage maps for BCG, Penta 3, and MCV1, district rankings showing Penta 1–3 dropout, monthly and annual doses administered, annual coverage trends, and comparisons of routine DPT3/MCV1 estimates against survey estimates.
Specifies that routine immunization coverage data must be disaggregated by vaccine, dose, and recipient age group (such as <1 year versus ≥1 year).

Explains that coverage for early schedule doses such as BCG or Penta-1 serves as an indicator of access to immunization services, where high first-dose coverage reflects both broad service reach and community acceptance of vaccination.

Explains why aggregate reporting systems rarely track 'fully immunized' children directly—given the difficulty of scanning complete individual immunization histories at facility level and evolving schedules across older ages—and instead rely on a tracer vaccine dose such as DTP3 to measure overall programme performance.

Notes that misclassifying children receiving their first or second DPT dose as receiving DPT3 can inflate reported DPT3 counts above DPT1, producing an apparent negative dropout rate even across a full year.

Recommends monitoring coverage for every vaccine in the national schedule to detect vaccine-specific uptake or programmatic issues early, especially following a new vaccine introduction to verify that uptake aligns with established vaccines.

Explains how age disaggregation distinguishes timely coverage (immunization before 12 months of age for infant vaccines, or before 24 months for MCV2 and in some countries MCV1) from delayed coverage (immunization at or after those age thresholds).

Advises against routine disaggregation of administered doses by sex, delivery strategy (fixed versus outreach), or catchment residency, noting that each added disaggregation doubles recording and reporting workload without yielding reliable or actionable routine data. It recommends streamlining facility reporting forms to limit cell counts and relying on household surveys for such questions.

Discusses target population denominators for coverage calculations, distinguishing live births for birth doses (BCG, OPV0, HepB0) from surviving infants for other first-year vaccines and preferring independent census-derived regional demographic estimates over national averages or local enumerations. It notes that coverage exceeding 100% signals either denominator underestimation (including cross-border or mobile populations) or over-reporting of administered doses.

Explains that abrupt year-to-year jumps or drops in coverage often stem from census-driven revisions to target population denominators, which can be diagnosed by graphing annual numerators and denominators separately rather than coverage percentages alone.
Provides the introductory lead-in fragment ('performance:') for the bulleted list of options to monitor immunization performance when reliable denominator estimates are lacking.

Lists denominator-independent performance monitoring options when target population estimates are unreliable, including tracking dropout rates and conducting nationwide or provincial/regional coverage evaluation surveys.

Explains how multi-year time series of doses administered and coverage estimates reveal both programme performance trends and data quality or denominator anomalies. It warns against interpreting coverage trends across years when facility reporting completeness has shifted substantially (e.g., from 65% to 85%) unless informed imputations for missing or invalid reports can be made in consultation with local staff.
Continues the guidance on data imputation for incomplete reporting, noting that analysts must assess whether facilities or months with missing data resemble those with valid reports.

Reviews the limitations and risks of household coverage surveys (such as DHS and MICS) when used as a benchmark against routine estimates, including multi-year measurement lags, wide uncertainty and small sample sizes at sub-national levels, variable interview and card-verification quality, parental recall bias, and unquantified non-sampling errors.
Displays the section heading continuation fragment ('IMMUNIZATION SCHEDULE') for the subsection on immunization dropouts.

Defines vaccine dropout rates (such as DTP1-to-DTP3 and MCV1-to-MCV2) as the percentage of children who start but fail to complete a vaccination course, serving as a key indicator of service utilization, service quality, and ability to vaccinate beyond the first year of life. It lists four standard tabular and graphical analyses (Charts/Tables 10–13) tracking annual and regional 12-month dropout rates.
Lists Chart 14 in the dropout analysis series, which classifies geographic regions based on two key performance indicators: DPT1 coverage and the DPT1-to-DPT3 dropout rate.

Describes how Figure 14 cross-classifies districts or provinces using DPT1 coverage thresholds (<90%, ≥90%, and >100%) and DPT1-to-DPT3 dropout rate categories (<10%, ≥10%, and negative dropout) to diagnose access, utilization, and data quality problems.

Introduces the vaccine stock management subsection covering monthly aggregate facility indicators for vaccine and injection supply availability and closed/open vial wastage. It outlines standard tables and charts (15–20) tracking the percentage of health facilities with full monthly availability by district and closed and open vial wastage rates by vaccine and region over 12-month and 5-year periods.

Lists the standard cold chain equipment monitoring analyses (Charts 21–23): monthly and annual counts of high and low temperature alarms by region, and monthly counts of functional refrigerators by region over the past 12 months.
Contains the running document header and page number ('WORKING DOCUMENT, FEBRUARY 2018 – 20 –') between the cold chain equipment charts and the stock management interpretation notes.

Defines 'full availability' of vaccines as meeting all vaccination demand without turning children away or providing incomplete schedules due to stockouts, emphasizing that health staff must track stock availability continuously whenever immunization is demanded rather than only checking end-of-month balances.

Defines closed vial wastage as the percentage of vaccine doses spoiled due to expiry, heat exposure (such as turned VVMs), freezing, or breakage, noting that while tracking wastage by reason code helps pinpoint storage or transport shortcomings, reliable reason-disaggregated data are difficult to obtain.

Provides the formula for open vial wastage—(doses used minus doses administered) divided by doses used, where doses used equals starting balance plus received doses minus ending balance—and explains that a negative wastage rate signals data quality errors from over-reported doses administered or under-reported doses used.

Explains that when digital temperature recorders are used, the counts of high and low temperature alarms over a reporting period provide a direct indicator of cold chain equipment performance and vaccine storage conditions.
Notes that tracking the number of functional refrigerators provides a basic indicator of health facility cold chain capacity.
Contains the running document header and page number ('WORKING DOCUMENT, FEBRUARY 2018 – 21 –') preceding the subsection on adverse events following immunization (AEFI).

Outlines the two-pronged monitoring approach for adverse events following immunization (AEFIs): monthly aggregate reporting of mild and severe AEFIs by facility and district, and individual case reporting and causality investigation for all severe/serious cases (involving hospitalization, disability, or death). It also lists standard regional and monthly/annual AEFI monitoring charts (24–26).
States the benchmark for AEFI surveillance sensitivity: reporting fewer than 10 AEFIs per year per 100,000 surviving infants suggests insufficiently sensitive AEFI surveillance.
Contains the running document header and page number ('WORKING DOCUMENT, FEBRUARY 2018 – 22 –') preceding the subsection on immunization sessions.

Explains the purpose of monitoring planned versus conducted immunization sessions (Chart 27) to help supervisors track micro-plan implementation and identify planning, operational, or budget constraints at reporting facilities.
Explains that monitoring reporting completeness (Charts 28–30) is essential for compiling and analysing routine immunization data and for accurately interpreting coverage trends over time.
Prompts analysts to verify whether complete district-level reporting actually includes reported vaccine doses from every underlying health facility within each district.
Advises analysts to examine regional differences in facility reporting completeness before interpreting apparent regional disparities in immunization coverage.

Title page and copyright notice for WHO's February 2018 working document 'Analysis and Use of Health Facility Data: Guidance for immunization programme managers' (Module 6).
